nameStory: The black-tipped darner gets its name from the distinctive dark markings at the tips of its wings, which look like someone dipped them in black ink. 'Darner' comes from the old belief that dragonflies could sew (or 'darn') people's mouths shut with their needle-like bodies - though of course, these gentle giants are completely harmless to humans!
description: The black-tipped darner is a large, impressive dragonfly that patrols New England's waters with powerful, direct flight. Like other darners, it's a substantial insect with a long, slender body and four strong, clear wings that shimmer in sunlight. These aerial acrobats are excellent hunters, catching mosquitoes and other small flying insects on the wing. Adults typically measure around 3 inches long with wingspans reaching nearly 4 inches.

idTips.label: Black wing tips
idTips.description: Look for distinct dark patches at the tips of all four wings - this is the most reliable field mark that separates it from other darners

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with strong, direct wingbeats in steady patrol routes over water, often at eye level or higher

idTips.label: Body coloration
idTips.description: Dark body with blue and green markings that shimmer in good light, appearing almost metallic when the sun hits just right

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Large and robust with a thick thorax (middle body section) that feels substantial if you gently catch one

idTips.label: Perching behavior
idTips.description: Often hangs vertically from branches or stems near water, wings held perpendicular to the body

habitat: Black-tipped darners favor clean lakes, ponds, and slow-moving streams throughout New England, especially those surrounded by woods or cattail marshes. You'll often spot them patrolling the edges where open water meets vegetation, typically in areas with good water quality since their aquatic larvae are sensitive to pollution.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from their aquatic larval stage in late spring, but are not yet at peak numbers. Look for freshly molted individuals with shiny, pristine wings.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when adults are most common and easiest to observe. They're actively hunting, mating, and laying eggs in warm, sunny weather.
seasonality.fall: Still active into early fall, especially on warm, sunny days. Some of the largest, most impressive individuals are seen during this season.
seasonality.winter: Adults have died off, but larvae continue developing underwater beneath the ice, preparing for next year's emergence.

funFact: Black-tipped darner larvae are underwater predators that can actually shoot water out of their rear ends like a jet engine to escape danger - it's called jet propulsion, and they're one of the few insects that use this rocket-like movement!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other large darners, but the black wing tips are usually diagnostic. If the wing tips aren't clearly visible, look for the combination of size, direct flight pattern, and preference for patrolling open water rather than flying through dense vegetation like some smaller dragonflies.
contextualKnowledge: Despite old folklore, dragonflies cannot sting or bite humans effectively - their strong jaws are designed for catching tiny flying insects, not for defense. The name 'darner' reflects ancient superstitions, but these insects are actually beneficial predators that help control mosquito populations.
compareHints: Among its darner relatives, the black wing tips make this species fairly distinctive. Canada darners lack the black wing tips and tend to be more blue-green, while shadow darners are typically darker overall and prefer more shaded areas. Variable darners have different wing markings and more interrupted color patterns on their bodies.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Aeshna relatives, the Shadow Darner stands out for its darker, more subdued coloration compared to species like the Green-striped Darner or Canada Darner, which show brighter blue and green markings.
Among its Aeshna relatives, the Canada Darner is most easily separated by its northern distribution and association with cooler, forested waters.
Among its Aeshna relatives in New England, the lance-tipped darner's male abdominal appendages are uniquely sharp and spear-like, while species like the Canada Darner have more rounded or blunt tips.

Among its darner relatives, the Green-striped Darner is the only one with such vivid green thoracic stripes - Canada Darners have blue markings, Shadow Darners are much darker overall, and Variable Darners have more mottled patterns.
Among its Aeshna relatives in New England, the Variable Darner stands out with its broken thorax stripes - most other darners in this genus have more continuous stripe patterns.
Among its Aeshna relatives in New England, the Lake Darner is most similar to the Canada Darner but distinguished by that black facial line.

Among New England's darners, the mottled darner stands out for its irregular, camouflaged patterning rather than the distinct stripes of the Canada Darner or the darker, more uniform coloration of the Shadow Darner.
